# Moderation and Interaction Effects {#sec-moderation} A moderator is a variable that changes the strength or direction of the relationship between a predictor and an outcome. In regression, we test moderation by adding an *interaction term*: the product of the predictor and the moderator. If the interaction is significant, the effect of the predictor depends on the level of the moderator. In this chapter, we build up an interaction model one step at a time. We start with continuous variables and then move to categorical ones. Along the way, we center predictors and use `ggeffects` to plot the predicted values that make interactions interpretable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(haven) library(psych) library(ggeffects) library(modelsummary) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Note:** These data are simulated to match a study of video game play and aggressive behavior (McNulty, 2015). ::: The data include 442 participants. The outcome is a measure of `aggression`. The predictor is `vidgames`, hours of video games played per week. The proposed moderator is `CaUnTs`, a score for callous-unemotional traits. We rename `CaUnTs` to something easier to type and save the result as a clean copy of the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} videogames <- read_dta("data/VideoGames.dta") videogames_clean <- videogames |> rename(callous = CaUnTs) describe(videogames_clean, fast = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## A model without an interaction We start with an ordinary multiple regression. Here, each predictor's effect is assumed to be the same at every level of the other predictor. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model1 <- lm(aggression ~ vidgames + callous, data = videogames_clean) summary(model1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = aggression ~ vidgames + callous, data = videogames_clean) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -27.952 -6.696 -0.168 7.022 32.499 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 21.76433 1.80731 12.042 < 2e-16 *** vidgames 0.18769 0.06940 2.705 0.00711 ** callous 0.76312 0.05024 15.191 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 10.13 on 439 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.3559, Adjusted R-squared: 0.353 F-statistic: 121.3 on 2 and 439 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Both predictors are positively related to aggression. However, this model cannot tell us whether the effect of video games is stronger for some participants than for others. ## Continuous predictor, continuous moderator To test whether `callous` moderates the effect of `vidgames`, we add their product to the model. In R, `vidgames * callous` expands to `vidgames + callous + vidgames:callous`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model2 <- lm(aggression ~ vidgames * callous, data = videogames_clean) summary(model2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = aggression ~ vidgames * callous, data = videogames_clean) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -29.7144 -6.9087 -0.1923 6.9036 29.2290 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 33.120233 3.427254 9.664 < 2e-16 *** vidgames -0.333597 0.150826 -2.212 0.027495 * callous 0.168949 0.161049 1.049 0.294731 vidgames:callous 0.027062 0.006981 3.877 0.000122 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 9.976 on 438 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.3773, Adjusted R-squared: 0.373 F-statistic: 88.46 on 3 and 438 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: The interaction term is positive and significant. This suggests that the relationship between video game play and aggression grows stronger as callous-unemotional traits increase. Notice that the coefficient for `vidgames` changed sign, from positive in Model 1 to negative here. Once an interaction is in the model, the coefficient for `vidgames` is no longer an "overall" effect. Instead, it is the effect of video games when `callous` equals zero. Very few participants score near zero on that scale, so this coefficient is not very meaningful on its own. ### Centering Centering fixes this interpretation problem. When we subtract the mean from each continuous predictor, zero becomes the sample average. Each lower-order coefficient then describes the effect of one predictor for a participant who is average on the other. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} videogames_clean <- videogames_clean |> mutate( vidgames_c = vidgames - mean(vidgames), callous_c = callous - mean(callous) ) model3 <- lm(aggression ~ vidgames_c * callous_c, data = videogames_clean) summary(model3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = aggression ~ vidgames_c * callous_c, data = videogames_clean) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -29.7144 -6.9087 -0.1923 6.9036 29.2290 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 39.967108 0.475057 84.131 < 2e-16 *** vidgames_c 0.169625 0.068473 2.477 0.013616 * callous_c 0.760093 0.049458 15.368 < 2e-16 *** vidgames_c:callous_c 0.027062 0.006981 3.877 0.000122 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 9.976 on 438 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.3773, Adjusted R-squared: 0.373 F-statistic: 88.46 on 3 and 438 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Compare Model 3 to Model 2. The interaction coefficient, its standard error, and the model *R*² are identical. Centering does not change the fit of the model. It only changes what the lower-order coefficients mean. In Model 3, the `vidgames_c` coefficient is the effect of one additional hour of video games for a participant with an average callousness score. The intercept is the predicted aggression score for a participant who is average on both predictors. ### Plotting the interaction Coefficients alone make interactions hard to see. A plot of predicted values is usually the clearest way to communicate one. `ggpredict()` computes predicted aggression across the range of `vidgames` at three values of `callous`: one standard deviation below the mean, the mean, and one standard deviation above it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred_cont <- ggpredict(model2, terms = c("vidgames", "callous [meansd]")) plot(pred_cont) + labs( title = NULL, x = "Video games (hours per week)", y = "Predicted aggression", color = "Callous-unemotional\ntraits" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-moderation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The lines fan out. Among participants low in callous-unemotional traits, video game play is almost unrelated to aggression. Among those high in these traits, the predicted aggression rises with each additional hour of play. ## Continuous predictor, categorical moderator Moderators are often categorical (for example, treatment and control groups). To demonstrate, we split `callous` into high (20 or above) and low groups. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Note:** Splitting a continuous variable into groups throws away information and reduces statistical power. We do it here only to show how a categorical moderator works. In your own work, keep a continuous moderator continuous. ::: We use `case_when()` to create the groups and `factor()` to give them labels. The first level listed becomes the reference group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} videogames_clean <- videogames_clean |> mutate( callous_group = case_when( callous >= 20 ~ "High", callous < 20 ~ "Low" ), callous_group = factor(callous_group, levels = c("Low", "High")) ) table(videogames_clean$callous_group) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Low High 250 192 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model4 <- lm(aggression ~ vidgames * callous_group, data = videogames_clean) summary(model4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = aggression ~ vidgames * callous_group, data = videogames_clean) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -30.9825 -6.3774 -0.0474 6.8175 30.8649 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 35.85328 2.23308 16.056 < 2e-16 *** vidgames -0.06529 0.09792 -0.667 0.505 callous_groupHigh -1.02189 3.31738 -0.308 0.758 vidgames:callous_groupHigh 0.63694 0.14453 4.407 1.32e-05 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 10.53 on 438 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.3064, Adjusted R-squared: 0.3016 F-statistic: 64.49 on 3 and 438 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: With a categorical moderator, the coefficients are easier to read directly: - `vidgames` is the slope for video games in the reference group (low callous). - `callous_groupHigh` is the difference between groups when `vidgames` equals zero. - `vidgames:callous_groupHigh` is how much steeper the video game slope is for the high callous group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred_cat <- ggpredict(model4, terms = c("vidgames", "callous_group")) plot(pred_cat) + labs( title = NULL, x = "Video games (hours per week)", y = "Predicted aggression", color = "Callous-unemotional\ntraits" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-moderation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Categorical predictor, categorical moderator When both variables are categorical, the interaction model is the same as a two-way ANOVA with an interaction (@sec-review). To demonstrate, we also split `vidgames` into high (22 or more hours per week) and low groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} videogames_clean <- videogames_clean |> mutate( vidgames_group = case_when( vidgames >= 22 ~ "High", vidgames < 22 ~ "Low" ), vidgames_group = factor(vidgames_group, levels = c("Low", "High")) ) model5 <- lm(aggression ~ vidgames_group * callous_group, data = videogames_clean) summary(model5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = aggression ~ vidgames_group * callous_group, data = videogames_clean) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -27.7745 -7.2507 -0.4094 6.5122 31.2255 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 35.488 0.954 37.200 < 2e-16 *** vidgames_groupHigh -2.078 1.338 -1.553 0.121 callous_groupHigh 8.034 1.468 5.475 7.4e-08 *** vidgames_groupHigh:callous_groupHigh 9.331 2.033 4.590 5.8e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 10.58 on 438 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.2997, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2949 F-statistic: 62.47 on 3 and 438 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Here, the intercept is the mean aggression score for the low/low group, and each coefficient adds a piece to that baseline. The interaction term is the extra difference found only in the high video games, high callous group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred_both <- ggpredict(model5, terms = c("vidgames_group", "callous_group")) plot(pred_both, connect_lines = TRUE) + labs( title = NULL, x = "Video game play", y = "Predicted aggression", color = "Callous-unemotional\ntraits" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-moderation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Lines that are not parallel indicate an interaction. Heavy video game play is associated with higher predicted aggression only in the high callous group. ## Summarizing the models ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} modelsummary( list( "Additive" = model1, "Continuous" = model2, "Centered" = model3, "Categorical moderator" = model4, "Both categorical" = model5 ), stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
